title: Async Python
intro: Async Python helps one process handle many waiting operations at once, especially network and database I/O. This topic teaches the event loop model, coroutines, task scheduling, cancellation basics, and practical rules for avoiding blocking calls. The goal is clear judgment: know when async is useful and how to apply it without introducing hidden complexity.
mental_model: Async code is cooperative concurrency. Coroutines run until an `await` point, then the event loop can run other ready tasks. This overlaps waiting time; it does not automatically speed up CPU-heavy calculations.
syntax:
import asyncio

async def fetch_user(user_id):
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    return {'id': user_id}

async def main():
    user = await fetch_user(10)
    return user

result = asyncio.run(main())
example:
import asyncio

async def fetch_all(ids):
    tasks = [fetch_user(i) for i in ids]
    return await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
must_know: `async def` defines a coroutine function; calling it returns a coroutine object.
`await` yields control so other tasks can progress while waiting.
The event loop schedules tasks and resumes them when awaited operations complete.
Use `asyncio.create_task` and `asyncio.gather` for concurrent task orchestration.
Avoid blocking calls like `time.sleep()` in async code paths.
common_traps: Forgetting to await a coroutine and assuming it already ran.
Mixing blocking sync I/O inside async routes or workers.
Assuming async means multi-core parallel CPU execution.
Launching tasks without tracking cancellation or error behavior.
Converting code to async when workload is CPU-bound.
interview: Explain concurrency vs parallelism clearly with an example.
Explain why blocking calls hurt event-loop throughput.
Show how gather/task orchestration works at a high level.
State when async should not be used.
real_world: API gateways use async I/O to overlap multiple downstream service calls within one request lifecycle.
Background workers can run many outbound checks concurrently without opening one OS thread per check.
outcome: By the end of this topic, you should be able to reason about coroutine lifecycle, event-loop scheduling, concurrency utilities, and when async architecture helps or hurts a design.

lesson_sections.title: 1. Coroutines and await
lesson_sections.body: `async def` creates coroutine functions. Calling one returns a coroutine object that must be awaited or scheduled. `await` marks yield points where the coroutine pauses so the event loop can run other tasks.

lesson_sections.title: 2. Event Loop Scheduling Model
lesson_sections.body: The event loop coordinates execution of asynchronous tasks. When a coroutine awaits I/O, control returns to the loop. This allows progress across many tasks in one thread while waiting operations complete.

lesson_sections.title: 3. Task Creation and gather
lesson_sections.body: Use `asyncio.create_task` for fire-and-track task scheduling and `asyncio.gather` for awaiting multiple coroutines together. Structured orchestration avoids ad-hoc concurrency bugs and makes error behavior explicit.

lesson_sections.title: 4. Cancellation and Timeouts
lesson_sections.body: Real systems need timeout and cancellation logic. Async tasks can be cancelled, and code should handle cancellation paths carefully to avoid partial state updates or hidden leaks.

lesson_sections.title: 5. Blocking Calls and Async Boundaries
lesson_sections.body: Blocking calls inside async code paths pause the event loop for all tasks. Prefer async-capable clients and adapters, and isolate unavoidable blocking work away from latency-sensitive async flows.

lesson_sections.title: 6. Choosing Async vs Sync
lesson_sections.body: Async is best for I/O-bound concurrency, not for heavy CPU workloads. Choose async when you need many overlapping waits. Choose sync when control flow is simple and throughput demands do not justify added complexity.
